name: Baking soda deodorant

lead: Baking soda deodorant uses sodium bicarbonate, alone or mixed with other ingredients, to manage underarm odour. It is one of the earliest patented deodorant ingredients and a common home recipe.
No published trials were found for it as a deodorant.

paras: It acts on odour, not sweat. It is mildly alkaline and is said to neutralise odour, though its general odour-absorbing effect has little evidence behind it.
Reference sources list eye irritation as its main hazard. Anecdotal reports of underarm irritation exist, but no published study of this was found.

lead: Baking soda deodorant refers to deodorants made with sodium bicarbonate, either commercial products or home-made mixtures applied to the underarms. Wikipedia lists sodium bicarbonate among the earliest patented deodorant ingredients and notes it appears in some dry and wet deodorants, alone or combined with other ingredients.[1][2]

Sodium bicarbonate is mildly alkaline in solution, and has long been promoted as an odour absorber, although the Wikipedia article on the compound says there is little evidence that it absorbs odours in general.[2] Patent literature includes a 2004 deodorant towelette system soaked in a solution that includes baking soda.[3]
No clinical studies of baking soda deodorants were found.

paras: Home-made versions mix baking soda with other ingredients, and some commercial natural deodorants include it. Body odour arises from bacterial breakdown of apocrine sweat; deodorants either mask odour or act on bacteria, and do not reduce sweat.[1][4]

Sodium bicarbonate, known since the 1801 work of Valentin Rose the Younger, is amphoteric, reacts with acids to release carbon dioxide, and gives mildly alkaline solutions.[2] Wikipedia's deodorant article discusses acid-based products as aimed at preserving the skin's slightly acidic acid mantle, and notes alkaline soaps can disrupt it.[1] Proponents of baking soda say it neutralises odour; no study located tested this on skin.

The main listed hazard of sodium bicarbonate on its reference page is serious eye irritation, and the page does not discuss skin irritation.[2] Some users on social media report underarm rashes from baking soda deodorants; the wiki located no published study of this.

timeline.event: Valentin Rose the Younger credited with discovering sodium bicarbonate in Berlin.[2]
US patent for a deodorant pad system using a baking soda solution.[3]
